title: The DOM and Browser Events
description: Understand the browser's live document tree, select and update elements, handle events, and build a data-driven DOM to-do list.
learningOutcomes: Explain how parsing creates distinct DOM node and element types.
Select nodes safely, traverse element relationships, and distinguish static from live collections.
Create and update nodes using safe text and attribute/property APIs.
Explain event target/currentTarget, capture/target/bubble, delegation and default actions.
Debug initial HTML attributes versus mutable DOM properties.
Build a data-driven DOM list and validate behavior with browser DevTools.
Choose between textContent, innerText and innerHTML, and drive classes and data attributes from one state object.
Choose a leading-edge throttle intentionally and remove its DOM event listener during teardown.

blocks.text: The DOM is the browser's live document model

The HTML source describes a document; the Document Object Model (DOM) is the structured tree the browser creates from that source. JavaScript can inspect or change that tree while the page is open. The DOM is neither a screenshot nor a frozen copy of the original HTML string: nodes can be added, removed, and updated after the browser finishes parsing.
Nodes and elements are related, not interchangeable

Every element is a node, but not every node is an element. An element such as a button has nodeType 1; text nodes have type 3; comments have type 8. For `
`, the panel's `childNodes` contains a comment and a button, while `children` contains only the button. Whitespace between tags can itself create text nodes, so counts change when formatting changes. Use element-specific traversal (`children`, `parentElement`, `nextElementSibling`) when you want element relationships; use `childNodes` only when text and comment nodes matter.

blocks.text: Select nodes and handle missing matches

document.querySelector(selector) returns the first matching element or null. document.querySelectorAll(selector) returns a static NodeList of all current matches. A static NodeList does not automatically include elements inserted after the query. Because a selector can match nothing, check a querySelector result before calling an element method on it.

blocks.text: Create and update nodes with focused APIs

Use createElement to create a node, classList to manage classes, setAttribute for attributes, textContent for plain text, append to insert nodes, and remove to detach one. These APIs keep content and structure separate. For user-provided strings, textContent is safer than interpreting that data as HTML.

blocks.title: Do not inject user input into innerHTML
blocks.text: innerHTML parses a string as markup. Concatenating untrusted input into it can enable cross-site scripting (XSS). Prefer createElement plus textContent for ordinary user text; only parse trusted or properly sanitized HTML when there is a clear reason.

blocks.text: HTML attributes and DOM properties can show different state

An HTML attribute is part of the element's markup/configuration; a DOM property is the JavaScript-facing state on the live object. For an input initially written with `value="hello"`, typing changes `input.value` but normally leaves `getAttribute("value")` and `defaultValue` at the initial value. A form reset restores the current value from its default. Some properties reflect attributes (for example `disabled`), but boolean attributes are true by their presence: `disabled="false"` still means disabled. Inspect the property that represents the state you actually need, and use DevTools Elements for markup attributes and Console for live properties.

steps.title: Observe the reset boundary
steps.explanation: form.reset() restores the current control value from its default value, which reflects the initial value attribute unless that default was changed.

blocks.text: Events connect user actions to code

addEventListener registers a callback that the browser runs when an element receives an event such as click, input, or submit. event.target identifies where the event originated; event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently running. Many events bubble to ancestors, making event delegation possible, but not every event bubbles.

blocks.text: Deep dive: event delegation, DOM collection behavior, and safe rendering

The DOM is a tree, so events can travel through capturing, target, and bubbling phases. Delegation uses bubbling: one stable parent listener handles actions on many current or future children. The event target may be a nested icon or span, not the button itself, so find the intended control with `closest()` and verify it belongs to the delegated container. For untrusted text, use `textContent`; `innerHTML` parses markup and can introduce injection risks.

blocks.text: Batch DOM work and choose the right browser observer

steps.title: Build nodes without interpreting strings as HTML
steps.explanation: Check the target before using it, then create elements and assign textContent. This keeps the label as text rather than parsing markup.

steps.title: Assemble a detached subtree
steps.explanation: DocumentFragment is a lightweight container for assembling nodes before insertion. Appending it moves its children into the document; the fragment itself is emptied.

steps.title: Commit the new list in one clear operation
steps.explanation: replaceChildren expresses that this list is replaced with the assembled items. A fragment can reduce repeated live-tree mutations and clarify intent, but do not promise a specific layout/reflow count—profile if performance matters.

blocks.text: Use an event listener when a known user or browser event occurs. Use MutationObserver when code needs to react to changes in a DOM subtree made by other code; its callback runs after mutations are queued, so avoid writing back in a way that creates an observation loop. Use IntersectionObserver to learn when a target approaches or enters a viewport/root, for tasks such as custom lazy loading or visibility analytics. Disconnect or unobserve when work is complete; native loading="lazy" is simpler for ordinary images.

steps.title: Select only targets with deferred sources
steps.explanation: The selector narrows work to images that declare the data attribute. The code still validates the dataset value before assigning it.

steps.title: Wait for proximity, then perform work once
steps.explanation: The callback receives entries and the observer. rootMargin starts loading before the image reaches the viewport; unobserve prevents repeated handling for the same image.

steps.title: Observe after setup and clean up on teardown
steps.explanation: Start observation after the callback exists. If a component or page region is removed, disconnect its observer to release observation work. For standard image deferral, compare this custom code with the simpler loading="lazy" attribute.

steps.title: Observe a specific subtree
steps.explanation: Choose the smallest element whose changes matter. A missing target should be handled before calling observe.

steps.title: Inspect records rather than polling
steps.explanation: MutationObserver batches mutation records for a later callback. Options define which changes to report; broad subtree/attribute observation can be noisy, so narrow them to the feature's need.

steps.title: Stop observation explicitly
steps.explanation: Disconnect when the feature unmounts or is done. If the callback itself changes observed nodes, ensure it converges instead of triggering an endless sequence of mutations.

steps.title: Define the event contract
steps.explanation: The event name and detail shape form a small contract between the producer and consumer. Keep it specific and document what the payload means.

steps.title: Dispatch from the component that owns the action
steps.explanation: CustomEvent carries application data in detail. Bubbling lets an ancestor listener handle it; custom events are not a replacement for React props/state inside a React-owned tree.

options.text: MutationObserver
options.feedback: MutationObserver reports DOM-tree or attribute changes, not viewport intersection.

options.text: IntersectionObserver
options.feedback: IntersectionObserver asynchronously reports intersection changes with a viewport or configured root.

options.text: A MutationEvent listener
options.feedback: Legacy mutation events are not the modern observer API and do not report viewport visibility.

options.text: setInterval checking getBoundingClientRect forever
options.feedback: Polling adds recurring work and lifecycle complexity; use the observer or native image loading when suitable.

blocks.explanation: Choose the API by the signal needed: DOM mutation, viewport intersection, or a known event.

items: Debounce waits until a burst of calls pauses; it fits search suggestions where only the final query should trigger work.
Throttle limits calls to at most a chosen cadence; it fits continuous signals such as scroll-driven updates when periodic work is needed.
Both require lifecycle cleanup when they wrap timers or listeners; cancel pending work when the component is removed.
Do not debounce every input indiscriminately: validation or feedback may need immediate response, and server requests still need cancellation/stale-response handling.

blocks.text: Throttle a scroll handler and clean it up

A leading-edge throttle lets the first event through, then skips further calls until the interval has elapsed. It fits repeated scroll/resize signals when periodic updates are useful. This version has no trailing timer: intermediate events, including a final event inside the interval, can be dropped. Choose a trailing-edge version or debounce when the final value must always be processed.

steps.title: Limit the call rate
steps.explanation: The wrapper records the last execution time and returns early when the interval has not elapsed. It is leading-edge only and schedules no trailing callback, so there is no pending timer to clear.

steps.title: Register a reusable listener
steps.explanation: The handler reads scroll position but never calls `preventDefault`, so a passive listener expresses that intent. Reuse the same function reference for removal.

steps.title: Remove the exact listener reference
steps.explanation: `removeEventListener` must receive the same callback reference and matching relevant options. Calling this disposer when the view is removed prevents the listener from retaining the handler and its closure.

blocks.prompt: This leading-edge throttle limits a scroll callback to at most once per 250 ms and does not create timers. What is the correct teardown?

options.text: Call `removeEventListener` with the same `handleScroll` function reference
options.feedback: Listener cleanup requires the original callback reference. This implementation creates no timer, so only the listener needs removal.

options.text: Create a new wrapper by calling `throttleLeading` again and pass it to `removeEventListener`
options.feedback: A newly created wrapper is a different function reference, so it will not remove the registered listener.

options.text: Call `clearTimeout` with the last timestamp
options.feedback: A timestamp is not a timer id, and this leading-only implementation does not schedule a trailing timer.

options.text: Do nothing because browsers remove all listeners as soon as a callback returns
options.feedback: Event listeners stay registered until removed or their target is collected; the page's window normally outlives the view.

blocks.explanation: A registered event listener stays active until it is removed or its target is collected. Retain and remove the exact callback reference; add timer cleanup only if the chosen throttle implementation actually schedules timers.

blocks.text: Navigate from a known node instead of querying again

Once you hold an element, the tree already links it to its relatives. Element-only properties (`parentElement`, `children`, `firstElementChild`, `lastElementChild`, `previousElementSibling`, `nextElementSibling`) skip text and comment nodes. Node-based properties (`parentNode`, `childNodes`, `firstChild`, `nextSibling`) include them, and indented markup creates whitespace text nodes between tags. Prefer the element-only forms unless you really need other node types. At the edges these properties return `null`, so guard before reading a property of the result. `closest(selector)` walks upward starting with the element itself and returns the first match or `null`; `parent.contains(node)` tests descendant relationships. Chains such as `parentElement.parentElement` couple code to the exact markup shape, so a `closest()` call with a meaningful selector or data attribute usually survives layout changes better.

steps.title: Start from one element you already hold
steps.explanation: The comment shows the markup and the single `querySelector` call that finds `.item-b`. Every relationship below is read from that node without another search of the document.

steps.title: Read element-only relationships
steps.explanation: Each property returns an Element or `null`. `children` is a live HTMLCollection containing only element children, so its length ignores text and comments. For the first or last item in a list, `previousElementSibling` or `nextElementSibling` is `null`, which must be handled.

steps.title: Notice the whitespace trap
steps.explanation: `firstChild` is the first node of any type. With indented markup it is usually a whitespace text node (nodeType 3), which has no `className`. `firstElementChild` skips non-element nodes and returns the element you meant.

steps.title: Search upward with closest
steps.explanation: `closest()` checks the element itself first, then each ancestor. That is why `closest('.item')` returns `current`. It returns `null` when nothing matches, which makes it the standard tool for event delegation.

blocks.prompt: A container's markup is indented across several lines. `container.firstChild.className` is `undefined`, although the first tag inside is a `div` with a class. What explains this, and what should you use?

options.text: `firstChild` returned a whitespace text node created by the indentation; use `firstElementChild` when you need an element
options.feedback: Text nodes have no `className`. Whitespace between tags is parsed into text nodes, and `firstChild` returns any node type.

options.text: `firstChild` only works after the page has finished loading, so wait for `DOMContentLoaded`
options.feedback: Timing is not the problem: the tree already exists, and the first node in it is simply not an element.

options.text: The HTML parser removes whitespace between tags, so the `div` should have been found
options.feedback: The parser keeps whitespace text nodes in most contexts, which is exactly why element-only properties exist.

options.text: `className` is only defined on elements after they have been attached to the document
options.feedback: `className` exists on any element, attached or not. The returned node was not an element.

blocks.explanation: The DOM contains text and comment nodes as well as elements. Use the element-only relationship properties when you mean elements, and guard against `null` at the edges.

blocks.text: Choose how text and markup are read and written

`textContent` reads or writes the exact text of every descendant text node. It includes text in hidden elements, does not parse markup, and is the default for showing user-visible text. `innerText` works with the rendered result: it respects CSS such as `display: none` and reflects layout line breaks, so reading it can require the browser to compute layout and is generally more costly. `innerHTML` serializes the children as a markup string when read and parses a string as HTML when written, replacing all existing children. `outerHTML` includes the element itself. A common security belief is that scripts inserted through `innerHTML` run; they do not, but event-handler attributes such as `onerror` on an `img` can, so any untrusted string must still be treated as dangerous. Writing `el.innerHTML += html` rebuilds every existing child, which discards listeners attached directly to them and any state they held, such as typed input.

steps.title: Set up markup and an untrusted string
steps.explanation: The element mixes visible text, a hidden element and a nested tag. The `input` string stands for user-supplied data that contains an event-handler attribute.

steps.title: Compare the three reads
steps.explanation: `textContent` returns all text, including the hidden span. `innerText` returns what a reader would see, so the hidden span is omitted. `innerHTML` returns markup, including tags and attributes. Choose the read that matches the question you are asking.

steps.title: Write untrusted data as text
steps.explanation: Assigning to `textContent` stores the string as a single text node. No `img` element is created, so `children.length` is 0 and the handler can never fire.

steps.title: Treat markup writes as rebuilds
steps.explanation: Assigning `innerHTML` parses a string and replaces every child. The `+=` form serializes the current children, concatenates, and parses again, so existing nodes are replaced with new ones. Use `append()` or `insertAdjacentElement()` with created nodes to add one item without rebuilding the rest.

blocks.prompt: A comment entered by a user must be displayed inside a paragraph. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assigning the string to `textContent` stores it as plain text and never parses markup
options.feedback: The value becomes a text node, so angle brackets are displayed literally.

options.text: Assigning to `innerText` also inserts text rather than markup, but reading `innerText` depends on rendering
options.feedback: Writes are treated as text, while reads reflect CSS and layout, which is why `textContent` is the simpler default for data.

options.text: Assigning to `innerHTML` is safe when the comment is short
options.feedback: Length does not matter. A short string such as an `img` with an `onerror` attribute is enough to run code.

options.text: `list.innerHTML += itemMarkup` is an efficient way to add one item
options.feedback: It serializes and re-parses every existing child, discarding their listeners and state.

options.text: A `<script>` tag assigned through `innerHTML` always executes, so only script tags need to be filtered
options.feedback: Scripts inserted this way do not run, but event-handler attributes can. Filtering one tag does not make parsing untrusted markup safe.

blocks.explanation: Use `textContent` for data. Parse HTML only from sources you control, with a reviewed policy, and add single items with created nodes rather than rebuilding a container.

blocks.text: Keep state in data, render it to the DOM, style it with CSS

`element.style` writes inline styles with camelCase names (`style.backgroundColor`) and reads only inline values. Inline declarations override ordinary stylesheet rules, so they are hard to change later from CSS. `getComputedStyle(el)` is read-only and returns resolved values after the cascade, such as `rgb(255, 0, 0)` or `24px`. For states such as open, active or selected, change a class or a data attribute and let CSS decide how it looks: `classList.add`, `remove`, `contains`, `replace`, and `toggle`. `toggle(name, force)` sets an explicit state, so the same call is safe to repeat, while a bare `toggle(name)` flips whatever the DOM currently holds. Assigning `className` replaces the entire class string. Performance does not come from using a class rather than `style`; it depends on which properties change, because properties such as `transform` and `opacity` can often be animated without layout, while width or top cannot. The pattern that scales is a state object that is the source of truth, a `render()` that writes it to text, attributes and classes, and event handlers that change state and then call `render()`.

steps.title: Declare one source of truth
steps.explanation: The state object holds the facts, not DOM nodes. The element references are looked up once and reused.

steps.title: Write the DOM only in render
steps.explanation: Text goes through `textContent`, the theme goes into a data attribute, and `toggle('open', state.isOpen)` sets the class from the state instead of flipping it. `aria-expanded` is updated in the same place so visual state and assistive-technology state cannot drift apart.

steps.title: Handlers change state, then render
steps.explanation: The click handler never touches the menu directly. It changes state and calls `render()`, so every code path produces the DOM from the same data.

steps.title: Render once at startup
steps.explanation: The first call makes the initial page match the state, including the `aria-expanded` value.

steps.title: Let CSS own appearance
steps.explanation: The stylesheet maps the data attribute and class to visuals. Changing the design means editing CSS, not JavaScript, and no inline style competes with these rules.

blocks.prompt: One handler calls `menu.classList.toggle('open')`, while other code sets `state.isOpen = false` without touching the menu. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: The class and the state can disagree, because a bare toggle flips whatever the DOM holds; set it from state with `toggle('open', state.isOpen)` inside `render()`
options.feedback: Deriving the DOM from state in one function keeps both in agreement, and repeating the call is harmless.

options.text: `classList.toggle` is deprecated, so the handler should assign `className` instead
options.feedback: `toggle` is current. Assigning `className` would also overwrite the other classes on the element.

options.text: Nothing: class changes are GPU-accelerated, so the DOM always catches up
options.feedback: Rendering speed does not synchronize state. Nothing connects the class to `state.isOpen` unless the code does.

options.text: `toggle` cannot take a second argument, so an `if` statement with `add` and `remove` is required
options.feedback: The optional second argument forces the result and is the cleaner way to write this.

blocks.explanation: A single render function that derives classes, attributes and text from state removes a whole category of synchronization bugs.

blocks.title: Build a safe, filterable card manager
blocks.context: A small page lists learning cards. Users add cards from a form, mark them done, delete them and filter by status. Every visible change must come from one state object, and the page must stay safe when a title contains markup.
instructions: Model state as an array of cards with `id`, `title`, `tag` and `done`, plus a `filter` of `all`, `active` or `done`.
Write `createCardElement(card)` with `createElement`, `textContent` and `dataset`; never interpolate a title or tag into an `innerHTML` string.

Write `render()` so it derives the visible cards from `state.filter`, rebuilds the grid with a DocumentFragment, shows an empty message, and syncs the filter buttons' `active` class and `aria-pressed`.
Attach one delegated click listener to the grid that finds `closest('[data-action]')`, checks it belongs to the grid, and toggles or deletes the card by its id in state.

Handle form submission with `preventDefault`, trimmed validation and a default tag, then clear the inputs, return focus to the title input and call `render()`. Wire the filter buttons to update `state.filter`.
requirements: All user-entered text is inserted with `textContent`; no user string is parsed as HTML.
State is the only source of truth: handlers change state and then call `render()`.
One listener covers the card actions, including cards added after the page loads.
Filtering derives a visible list and never mutates `state.cards`.
Empty or whitespace-only titles are rejected without adding a card, and filter buttons expose their pressed state.
hints: Read the action and the id from `closest('[data-action]')`, not from `event.target`, because a click can land on an icon inside the button.
Compute `visible` with `filter()`; do not splice or sort `state.cards` just to display a filter.
`grid.replaceChildren(fragment)` clears and inserts in one call; render an empty-state paragraph when `visible` is empty.
Test with the title ``; it must appear as literal text and run nothing.
successCriteria: Adding, completing, deleting and filtering cards all update the page from state alone.
The hostile-title test is displayed literally and executes no code.
Cards added after load respond to actions without registering new listeners.
Filter buttons and the empty message stay correct after every action.

items: Use element-only relationship properties for elements, guard against `null`, and prefer `closest()` over chains of `parentElement`.
`textContent` is for data, `innerText` reflects rendered text, and `innerHTML` parses markup and rebuilds every child.
Keep state in data, write the DOM in one `render()`, use `classList.toggle(name, force)` and data attributes, and let CSS own appearance.
Delegation relies on bubbling; explicitly resolve nested targets and validate container ownership.
DOM selectors differ in whether their collections are static or live.
Insert untrusted text with textContent and use HTML parsing only with an intentional, reviewed policy.
